title: Strengthening an Argument
theme: Rhetoric: rebuttal, qualification and the strongest case
objectives: I can name the moves that make an argument stronger: preempting, bolstering, qualifying, and rebutting.
I can judge how well a claim is supported using words such as tenuous and indisputable.
I can explain how an analogy, a euphemism, and an understatement shape a reader's response.
I can write a short persuasive paragraph that answers an objection, using at least four words from this unit.
rationale: This second rhetoric unit shifts from analyzing persuasion to writing it. The ten words name the moves of a mature argument (preempt, bolster, caveat, objection, rebuttal), the language for judging how well a claim stands (tenuous, indisputable), and three figures that change how a statement lands (analogy, euphemism, understatement). Students already know the appeals from the first rhetoric unit; here they learn that a strong writer anticipates the other side and says exactly how far a claim goes. The passage is a speech so that students can hear and mark each move.

words.def: A reply that argues against a claim or criticism, usually by giving evidence.
words.ex: In the debate, Imani's rebuttal used the other team's own statistics to show a gap in their claim.
words.ex2: Her written rebuttal to the editorial listed three facts that the author had left out.
words.nonExample: Saying no, you are wrong, without giving a reason is not a real rebuttal.

apps.academic: In a debate, the rebuttal round gives each team a chance to answer the other side's evidence.
apps.spoken: Let me offer a rebuttal to that point.
apps.writing: A strong rebuttal names the claim it answers and then gives evidence against it.

cloze.s: After the opposing team finished, Imani stood up and gave a sharp ___ that used their own numbers against them.

cloze2.s: The editor published a ___ to the column, answering each of its three main claims with evidence.

misuse.s: Her rebuttal agreed with every point the other side made and added nothing new.
misuse.why: A rebuttal argues against a claim; agreeing with every point does not answer or oppose anything.

visual.alt: A speech bubble beside an arrow that points back.

words.frame: A strong rebuttal to the claim that ___ would say ___.

words.def: A reason or statement that expresses disagreement with an idea, a plan, or a claim.
words.ex: Her main objection to the plan was that it would cost more than it saved.
words.ex2: The lawyer raised an objection, and the judge asked her to explain her reason.
words.nonExample: Quietly nodding along with a plan is not an objection.

apps.academic: A good argument answers the strongest objection before the reader has a chance to raise it.
apps.spoken: I have one objection: we have not heard from the neighbors.
apps.writing: State the objection fairly in your own words before you answer it.

cloze.s: The council member's only ___ to the park plan was that it would remove the community garden.

cloze2.s: Before accepting the proposal, the committee asked whether anyone had an ___ to it.

misuse.s: Her objection to the plan was that she thought it was excellent and wanted it passed at once.
misuse.why: An objection expresses disagreement; praising a plan and asking for it to pass is approval.

visual.alt: A raised hand beside a question mark.

words.frame: A fair objection to ___ is that ___.

words.def: A warning or condition that limits or qualifies a statement.
words.ex: The scientist offered one caveat: the results came from a small sample of twenty students.
words.ex2: I support the new schedule, with one caveat: it must include time for lunch.
words.nonExample: An outright promise with no conditions attached carries no caveat.
words.rel: a limit placed on a claim

apps.academic: A responsible report states its caveats, such as the size of the sample and what was not measured.
apps.spoken: Sure, you can borrow it, with one caveat: bring it back by Friday.
apps.writing: Place a caveat next to the claim it limits, using words such as however or provided that.

cloze.s: The coach said the team would play in the final, with one ___: the star player had to pass her medical exam first.

cloze2.s: The report's most important ___ was that the survey had asked only students at one school.

misuse.s: The manager's caveat added no condition at all, and she promised everything without any limits.
misuse.why: A caveat is a warning or condition; a promise with no conditions has none.

visual.alt: A warning triangle beside a handwritten note.

words.frame: I agree with ___, with one caveat: ___.

words.def: To deal with something in advance so that it cannot be used against you or cannot happen.
words.ex: The speaker tried to preempt criticism by admitting the plan's flaws before anyone else could mention them.
words.ex2: The city preempted flooding by clearing the storm drains before the rainy season.
words.nonExample: Waiting for a critic to speak and then replying is not preempting.
words.rel: acting before the other side can

apps.academic: Good writers preempt objections by addressing them before the reader can raise them.
apps.spoken: I want to preempt a question: yes, we checked the data twice.
apps.writing: To preempt an objection, state it fairly and answer it in the same paragraph.

cloze.s: The student began her speech by naming the biggest weakness in her plan, hoping to ___ the audience's strongest objection.

cloze2.s: The mayor acted to ___ a bigger crisis by repairing the weak levee before the spring floods arrived.

misuse.s: To preempt the argument, she waited until her opponent had finished speaking and the debate was over.
misuse.why: To preempt is to act before something happens; waiting until the debate is over is too late.

visual.alt: A raised hand in front of a shield.

words.frame: I could preempt the objection that ___ by saying ___.

words.def: To strengthen or support something so that it is harder to challenge.
words.ex: The writer cited three new studies to bolster her claim.
words.ex2: A strong finish bolstered the team's confidence before the playoffs.
words.nonExample: Contradicting your own evidence does not bolster a claim; it weakens it.

apps.academic: Evidence, examples, and expert opinion can all bolster a claim.
apps.spoken: A good night's sleep will bolster your confidence.
apps.writing: Say what bolsters a claim and how: a statistic, an example, or an expert.

cloze.s: To ___ her argument, the student added a statistic and a quotation from the school nurse.

cloze2.s: The coach tried to ___ the team's confidence by reminding players of how far they had come this season.

misuse.s: He bolstered his argument by ignoring all the evidence and relying only on guesses.
misuse.why: To bolster is to strengthen; ignoring evidence and guessing weakens an argument.

visual.alt: A stack of bricks beside a flexed arm.

words.frame: I can bolster my claim by ___.

words.def: Weak or thin, with little support; easily broken.
words.ex: The connection between the two events was so tenuous that the judge refused to allow it as evidence.
words.ex2: Her tenuous grasp of the topic showed when she could not explain her own conclusion.
words.nonExample: A claim supported by five independent studies is not tenuous.

apps.academic: A tenuous link between a cause and an effect is not enough to prove causation.
apps.spoken: He holds a tenuous lead, so he cannot relax yet.
apps.writing: Use tenuous for a weak connection or a thinly supported claim, not for something that is merely small.

cloze.s: The lawyer called the connection between the defendant and the crime too ___ to convince a jury.

cloze2.s: A ___ friendship, built on one chance meeting, ended when both of them moved away.

misuse.s: The evidence was so tenuous that three experts and five studies confirmed it beyond question.
misuse.why: Tenuous means thin and weakly supported; a claim confirmed by many experts is solid.

visual.alt: A single thin thread with scissors about to cut it.

words.frame: A tenuous claim is one that ___.

words.def: So clearly true that it cannot be argued against.
words.ex: The fingerprints on the glass were indisputable proof that she had been in the room.
words.ex2: The size of the crowd was indisputable, since the stadium was visibly full.
words.nonExample: A rumor passed from friend to friend is not indisputable.

morph.note: The final e of dispute is dropped before -able.

apps.academic: Historians call a fact indisputable only when many independent sources agree.
apps.spoken: It is indisputable that she worked harder than anyone else on the team.
apps.writing: Reserve indisputable for claims you can back with overwhelming evidence.

cloze.s: The video was ___ evidence that the car had run the red light, since both the time stamp and the signal were clearly visible.

cloze2.s: The rain was ___: everyone in the room could see the water streaming down the windows.

misuse.s: Because the claim was indisputable, nearly every expert argued against it and no evidence supported it.
misuse.why: Indisputable means too clear to argue against; a claim that experts reject is not.

visual.alt: A check mark beside a balanced scale.

words.def: A comparison between two things that shows how they are alike in an important way, used to explain or argue a point.
words.ex: The teacher used an analogy, comparing the heart to a pump, to explain how blood moves through the body.
words.ex2: A weak analogy compares two things that are alike on the surface but different in the ways that matter.
words.nonExample: Saying two things are both blue is not an analogy unless the color helps explain a point.

apps.academic: An analogy can explain a hard idea, but test it by asking where the comparison breaks down.
apps.spoken: Here is an analogy: learning to code is like learning a new language.
apps.writing: State the two things, say what they share, and note one limit of the comparison.

cloze.s: To explain how the immune system works, the doctor used an ___ comparing white blood cells to security guards.

cloze2.s: The author's ___ between a country's budget and a family's budget helped readers understand the idea, though it left out important differences.

misuse.s: An analogy is a list of facts about a single subject, with no comparison to anything else.
misuse.why: An analogy compares two things; a list about one subject has nothing to compare.

visual.alt: Two shapes joined by lines that show what they have in common.

words.frame: An analogy for ___ is ___ because both ___.

words.def: A mild or polite word used in place of one that sounds harsh or unpleasant.
words.ex: Saying that someone passed away is a euphemism for saying that the person died.
words.ex2: The company called the layoffs a workforce adjustment, a euphemism that hid how many people lost their jobs.
words.nonExample: Saying the soup is cold when it is cold is plain speech, not a euphemism.
words.rel: a gentle word for a hard truth

apps.academic: Critics identify euphemisms when a text uses gentle words to soften a harsh fact.
apps.spoken: Between jobs is a euphemism for unemployed.
apps.writing: Notice whether a euphemism is kind or whether it hides the truth.

cloze.s: The notice called the canceled program a schedule realignment, a ___ that hid the fact that students were losing it.

cloze2.s: Between jobs is a common ___ for being out of work.

misuse.s: He used a euphemism by shouting the harshest word he could think of.
misuse.why: A euphemism softens a harsh idea; shouting the harshest word does the opposite.

visual.alt: A speech bubble decorated with flowers.

words.frame: A euphemism for ___ is ___, which sounds ___.

words.def: A statement that describes something as much smaller or less serious than it really is.
words.ex: Calling the hurricane a bit of wind was a huge understatement.
words.ex2: Her teammates said it would be an understatement to say she had improved this season.
words.nonExample: Calling a blizzard the worst snowstorm in a century is not an understatement.

morph.note: A compound of under and statement.

apps.academic: Understatement is a rhetorical tool that makes a serious fact stand out by treating it calmly.
apps.spoken: Saying it was warm today would be an understatement; it was boiling.
apps.writing: Set an understatement beside clear facts so that readers notice the gap between the words and the truth.

cloze.s: Saying the runners were a little tired after twenty-six miles was an ___.

cloze2.s: It was an ___ to call the repair bill a small expense when it cost more than the car was worth.

misuse.s: Calling a tiny scratch the end of the world was a perfect understatement.
misuse.why: An understatement says less than the truth; calling a scratch the end of the world says far more.

visual.alt: A line from 'much less than the truth' to 'much more than the truth', with understatement at the low end.

words.frame: Calling ___ just ___ would be an understatement because ___.

passage.title: Keep the Library Open
paras: Members of the board, I am asking you to keep our school library open until 5:30 on weekdays. Before I make my case, I want to preempt the first question you will ask, which is about cost. The library aide's contract already runs until 5:00, so the extra half hour would cost the district less than the price of one new textbook each week.

Some people will say that students can study at home. This objection deserves a serious answer, and here is my rebuttal. In a survey by our student council, one in four students in our grade said they have no quiet place or reliable internet at home. For them, the library is not a convenience. It is the only place where homework can be finished.

To bolster my argument, let me offer an analogy. A library is like a bridge: nobody thinks about it when it is open, but anyone who needs to cross it when it is closed is stranded. A bridge that closes at three o'clock helps only the people whose day ends at three.

I must admit one caveat. Longer hours will not help students who cannot stay because of the bus schedule. That is why I also ask the board to consider a late bus on two afternoons a week. Without it, my claim that the library helps everyone would be tenuous, a promise that reaches only half of the students it names.

Finally, the district's notice says that the library is being optimized. That is a euphemism for cutting hours, and students deserve plain words. The notice also calls the change a minor adjustment, which is an understatement: for the students I have described, it is the loss of their only quiet room. The effect is indisputable. After the library closed early in October, teachers recorded that fewer homework assignments were turned in. I ask the board to vote yes, not because the plan is perfect, but because the need is real.

qs.q: In paragraph 1, the speaker says she wants to “preempt” the question about cost. She means that she will
choices: ignore the question completely
ask the board to repeat the question
answer the question before anyone asks it
apologize for the cost of the plan
qs.why: Preempt means to deal with something in advance. She answers the cost question right away, before the board can raise it.

qs.q: Why does the speaker compare the library to a bridge?
choices: To show that a service matters most to the people who need it at the moments when it is closed.
To suggest that the school should build a new bridge.
To prove that libraries are older than bridges.
To argue that students should walk home instead.
qs.why: The analogy says that people notice a bridge only when they cannot cross, just as students who need the library are stranded when it is closed.

qs.q: Which detail best bolsters the claim that the library is a necessity for some students?
choices: The aide's contract already runs until 5:00.
The library closes at 3:30 on Fridays.
The district's notice used the word optimized.
One in four students said they have no quiet place or reliable internet at home.
qs.why: The survey result shows that a large share of students depend on the library to finish homework.

qs.q: Why does the speaker admit the caveat about bus schedules?
choices: She has decided to withdraw her request.
She wants to be honest about a limit and offer a fix, which makes the argument harder to dismiss.
She believes the board will not read the survey.
She hopes the board will cancel the late bus.
qs.why: By naming the weakness and proposing a late bus, she answers the objection before the board raises it.

qs.q: Why does the speaker call “a minor adjustment” an understatement?
choices: The change affects only the school aide.
The notice exaggerates the cost of the library.
The change is far more serious for some students than the phrase suggests.
The notice was written in a very polite voice.
qs.why: She explains that for the students without a quiet room at home, the closing is the loss of their only place to study.

sentences: Write a sentence that preempts an objection to a rule at your school. Name the objection.
Write a sentence that uses caveat to limit a claim about homework or sleep.

given: The claim rested on one story.
combine.model: Because the claim rested on a single secondhand story, it was tenuous.

given: She gave a fix for the limit.
combine.model: The writer admitted a caveat and offered a fix for it, which bolstered her argument.

discuss: Is it better to preempt an objection or to answer it in a rebuttal after someone raises it? Why?
When is a euphemism kind, and when is it dishonest? Use euphemism in your answer.
Can an analogy ever prove a claim, or does it only explain one?
produce.explain: Explain how a caveat can make an argument stronger instead of weaker. Use caveat and one other word from the unit.

argue.prompt: Claim: Students should be allowed to choose their own seats in every class. Take a side and write an argument that preempts one objection and bolsters your claim with two reasons.
argue.frame: I believe that ___ because ___. Some people might object ___, but ___. In addition, ___.

constructed.prompt: A student wants the school to start a recycling club. Name the most likely objection and show how the student could preempt it. Use both words.
look: names a realistic objection such as cost or time
shows an answer given in advance
constructed.model: The main objection is that the club would cost too much. The student could preempt it by saying at the start that the bins can be donated and the club needs no budget.

constructed.prompt: A classmate claims that a certain brand of sneakers makes students faster, but the only evidence is one race. Explain why the claim is tenuous and how the classmate could bolster it.
look: says one race is thin evidence
suggests a stronger kind of evidence such as repeated tests
constructed.model: The claim is tenuous because one race is too little evidence. The classmate could bolster it by timing many runners in both kinds of shoes on several days.

constructed.prompt: Explain the difference between a euphemism and an understatement, and give one example of each.
look: gives a clear example of each
constructed.model: A euphemism is a gentle word for something harsh, such as passed away for died. An understatement says less than the truth, such as calling a flood a little water.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words for building and judging an argument, then use them to read a speech and write their own. The unit follows the first rhetoric unit by asking students to produce persuasion: anticipate the other side, qualify their claim, and support it. It also gives three figures (analogy, euphemism, understatement) that shape tone and show up in speeches and editorials.

notes.va.rebuttal.n: A rebuttal answers a claim with evidence. Have students mark the rebuttal in the passage (paragraph 2). Students may confuse rebuttal with refusal; stress that a rebuttal gives a reason. The verb is rebut.
notes.va.objection.n: An objection is a reason against an idea. Ask students to turn a complaint into an objection by adding a reason. Note that object as a verb and as a noun (a thing) is pronounced differently.
notes.va.caveat.n: A caveat is a limit placed on a claim, and a good writer uses it to be exact. The word is Latin for let him beware, as in caveat emptor; mention only if students are curious. Practice with sentences that use except, unless, and provided that.
notes.va.preempt.v: Preempt means to deal with something in advance. Use the pre- (before) clue. In writing, to preempt is to state an objection fairly and answer it before the reader raises it. Students sometimes confuse it with interrupt; have them write both meanings.
notes.va.bolster.v: Bolster is a strong verb for supporting a claim. Ask students what can bolster a claim (evidence, examples, expert testimony) and what undermines one. The review word undermine is the opposite action.
notes.va.tenuous.adj: Tenuous is figurative when applied to a claim: thin and easily broken, like a thread. Show students a weak argument and a thread. Do not let students use it for something merely small.
notes.va.indisputable.adj: Indisputable is in- (not) plus dispute plus -able. Students overuse it; ask them what evidence would justify the word. Contrast with undeniable and obvious. The final e of dispute is dropped.
notes.va.analogy.n: An analogy explains one thing through another. Every analogy has limits, so ask where each one breaks down. Distinguish from metaphor: an analogy usually explains in more detail and has a purpose. Link to the analogy items in the unit.
notes.va.euphemism.n: A euphemism softens something harsh. Ask students whether each euphemism is kind or evasive. Use classroom examples carefully; avoid pointing to anyone's situation. Connect to credibility: a euphemism that hides the truth can damage trust.
notes.va.understatement.n: Understatement says less than the truth, often with humor or calm force. It is a compound of under and statement. Have students rewrite a bold exaggeration as an understatement and describe the effect.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: “The speaker begins by preempting the cost question, so she shows she has thought about the other side. In paragraph 2 she states the objection and gives a rebuttal with a survey as evidence. The analogy of the bridge bolsters her claim by making the need vivid. Her caveat about buses makes the argument more honest, and it keeps the claim from being tenuous.”
discuss: Which move in the speech is the most persuasive, and why?
How does admitting a limit make a speaker more believable?
Where does the bridge analogy break down?
misconceptions: A caveat is a mistake in an argument.
A euphemism is always a lie.
An understatement is the same as a lie.
A rebuttal can be just a disagreement.
extend: Rewrite a short editorial so that it preempts one objection and adds one caveat.
Collect three euphemisms from news or advertising and decide what each hides or softens.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Bring back rhetoric, cogent, undermine and logos when students label the moves in the speech. Revisit preempt and caveat after two days with a short paragraph of their own, and use analogy and understatement in later literary analysis.

To bolster my claim, I will add ___.
wida.oral: Partner A states a claim about a school rule. Partner B gives one objection. Partner A answers with a rebuttal, and both partners say which word from the unit names each move.

needsReview: Spanish glosses not reviewed by a native speaker: refutación/réplica (rebuttal), objeción, salvedad (caveat), adelantarse a/prevenir (preempt), reforzar (bolster), tenue/débil, indiscutible, analogía, eufemismo, atenuación/subestimación (understatement).
Teacher note for caveat says the word is Latin for let him beware; confirm against a dictionary.
Passage is a fictional speech: the survey, the district notice and the teacher records are invented for the scenario and are not presented as real data.
Morphology: preempt and rebuttal are not segmented; no etymology is claimed beyond pre- (before) in the teacher notes; indisputable is segmented as in- + dispute + -able.
Sense boundary: preempt is taught in the sense of dealing with something in advance (not the legal sense of taking priority).
